title: Ten sayings (Avot 5:1)
hook: the world was made with ten sayings, so that each life counts
tomorrow: what did God make at sunset, right before the first Shabbat?

segments.voice: Yesterday, against your will: born, living, dying, and still an account. Given, and still accountable. Today chapter five opens, at the very beginning.

Some things could be done in one step and aren't. A letter written by hand instead of a text. A cake from scratch instead of a box. Avot notices that about the world itself. Genesis tells creation as a string of sayings: and God said, and God said. Chapter five opens by counting ten of them, then asks the question a kid would ask. Couldn't it have been made with one?
screen: `ONE STEP, OR MANY?` → `AND GOD SAID, AND GOD SAID.` → `COULDN'T ONE HAVE DONE IT?`

segments.voice: The mishnah answers itself. Ten, so the world would weigh more: so the wicked, who destroy a world made with ten sayings, pay for it, and the righteous, who sustain a world made with ten sayings, get good reward. Something to tell a friend tonight: count the and God saids in Genesis one and you get nine. The Talmud noticed, and says in the beginning is a saying too. Now the two readings, because people lean two ways on one sentence. One side hears a warning. The world was made with care, step by step, so breaking any part of it is serious; carelessness costs more than it looks. The other side hears an invitation. If the world took ten sayings, then holding up even a small piece of it, a meal, a kept promise, a kind word, carries that weight too. The mishnah puts both in one breath and doesn't choose. Another mishnah, in Sanhedrin, makes it personal. One person was created alone, it says, to teach that whoever destroys one life is as if they destroyed a whole world, and whoever sustains one life, as if they sustained a whole world. And one more reason: so no one could say to another, my ancestor is greater than yours. Everyone goes back to the same one.
screen: `TEN, SO THE WORLD WEIGHS MORE.` · `NINE, AND IN THE BEGINNING.` · `A WARNING, OR AN INVITATION?` · `ONE LIFE, A WHOLE WORLD.` · then, large: `TEN SAYINGS.`

segments.voice: Say one good sentence out loud, about someone in your life, plainly, the way you'd say it to their face. Then another, about someone else. Keep going for as long as the sit holds, up to ten, each one a small saying that holds a piece of the world up.
screen: `ONE GOOD SENTENCE, OUT LOUD.` · `THEN ANOTHER.` · `UP TO TEN.`

segments.voice: Ten sayings: the words of creation in Genesis, and God said. Ten, the mishnah says, so the world would weigh.
A line for the road: ten sayings, so what you break and what you hold up both count. That's chapter five, begun.

howItsDone: Pirkei Avot is read on summer Shabbat afternoons, a chapter a week; chapter five's numbered sayings, of tens, sevens and fours, are often studied in pairs, with partners arguing over each reading.

chat.meaning: The world was made with ten sayings so each part weighs, and Sanhedrin says one life is a whole world. Small parts count.

Avot.meaning: Pirkei Avot: the sages' sayings, chapters of the fathers

Sanhedrin.meaning: a tractate of the Mishnah about courts and judges

Talmud.meaning: the rabbis' long discussion built on the Mishnah

Genesis.meaning: the first book of the Torah, where creation is told

notes: Avot 5:1 paraphrased: with ten sayings the world was created; could it not have been created with one? To exact payment from the wicked who destroy, and give good reward to the righteous who sustain, a world created with ten sayings.
Debate: the 'warning' and 'invitation' readings are presented as two ways readers lean, not attributed to named commentators. Confirm this is fair.
Rosh Hashanah 32a / Megillah 21b: the ten sayings counted as nine 'and God said' plus 'In the beginning' (with Psalm 33:6). Confirm.

Sanhedrin 4:5: some texts read 'one soul of Israel'; others (e.g. the Kaufmann manuscript) read 'one soul'. Script says 'one life', following the universal reading; the 'no one can say my ancestor is greater than yours' line is in the same mishnah. Unity thread (one human race) noted for the owner.
